props.title: Come See the Paradise
props.initialSlug: Love in the face of tragedy.

sections.content: **Come See the Paradise** (1990) stands as one of Hollywood's most poignant examinations of Japanese-American internment during WWII. Director Alan Parker crafts an intimate love story against the backdrop of systemic racism and wartime hysteria, similar to how **Snow Falling on Cedars** (1999) would later approach the subject. Dennis Quaid and Tamlyn Tomita deliver powerful performances as an interracial couple torn apart by Executive Order 9066, with Parker's characteristic attention to period detail evident in every frame.

sections.content: Parker's film arrived during a crucial period of Japanese-American historical recognition, following President Reagan's Civil Liberties Act of 1988 which formally apologized for internment. This timing aligns with other films addressing previously ignored aspects of Asian-American history, like **The Joy Luck Club** (1993) and **A Family Gathering** (1988). The film's structure, moving between 1936 and 1942, effectively shows how quickly established American lives could be destroyed by government policy.

The film's technical achievements deserve special mention. Michael Seresin's cinematography captures both the vibrant pre-war Little Tokyo scenes and the stark desolation of the Manzanar internment camp. This visual approach influenced later historical dramas like **American Pastime** (2007) and **Under the Blood Red Sun** (2014), which also dealt with Japanese-American experiences during WWII. sections.content: **Come See the Paradise** (1990) helped pave the way for more nuanced Asian-American stories in mainstream cinema. While earlier films like **Bad Day at Black Rock** (1955) touched on anti-Japanese sentiment, Parker's film marked one of the first major studio productions to center Japanese-American characters as full protagonists. This shift influenced later works like **Better Luck Tomorrow** (2002) and **The Terminal Island** (2004), which continued exploring Asian-American identity in different contexts.
